slides.title: Probability and Bayes
slides.main: Every day consists of random events that can be reasoned about strictly.

captions: Probability and Bayes' theorem — the final chapter of the course
This is the most honest way to think in a world where nothing is guaranteed
A cache hits or misses, a feature wins or doesn't, an alert is real or false — all of this can be reasoned about strictly
We will go through classical probability, conditional probability and Bayes' formula — and sum up the whole journey
I promise: the spam filter at the end will be well deserved

frames.text: and the summary of the whole journey
at the end of the chapter — well deserved

body.text: The final chapter of the course: caches, A/B tests and alerts live on these formulas.

slides.title: Classical probability
slides.main: Probability is the share of favorable outcomes among all equally likely ones.

captions: The classical definition is almost naive
If all outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the share of favorable outcomes among all of them
A die has 6 faces: the probability of an even number is 3 out of 6, that is 1/2
A coin has two outcomes: the probability of tails is 1/2
When there are many outcomes, counting the shares without the counting rules from the first chapters is no longer possible

body.text: As soon as the outcomes become many, counting their shares without the counting rules from the first chapters is no longer possible.

slides.title: The combinatorics of chance
slides.sub: Not a guest but the hostess
slides.main: Intuition about randomness is unreliable, while counting formulas are reliable.

captions: Combinatorics here is not a guest but the hostess
Toss five coins: all outcomes 2⁵ = 32 — each coin doubles the options
Choosing a starting five from twenty — C(20, 5) = 15 504; without the formula you would count until evening
The birthday paradox: in a room of 23 people the probability of a match is above 50 %, since there are almost 250 pairs
Intuition about randomness is unreliable, while counting formulas are reliable

frames.text: count in order to know the probability

slides.title: Events: or and and
slides.main: The probability of "or" is the sum of the probabilities minus the probability of "and".

captions: Next — events and the arithmetic over them
The probability of "the first or the second" is the sum of the probabilities minus the probability of both: otherwise the common cases would be counted twice
The probability of "both" depends on the link between the events — that is the next conversation
"A database error or a network error" is a union; "a database error and the retries exhausted" is an intersection
Write the event in words — and the formula assembles itself

body.text: The minus is for the common cases: without it, those who fell into both categories would be counted twice. Write the event in words — the formula assembles itself.

slides.title: Independence of events
slides.sub: Knowing one changes nothing in the estimate of the other
slides.main: For independent events the probability of both at once is the product.

captions: Events are independent if knowing about one changes nothing in the estimate of the other
Two dice: a six came up on the first — about the second we still know only "one sixth"
For independent events the probability of both is the product: 1/6 · 1/6 = 1/36
Do not confuse independence with incompatibility: "even" and "three" are incompatible, but dependent
Dependence is about information, not about simultaneity

body.text: Dependence is about information, not about simultaneity.

slides.title: Conditional probability
slides.sub: The main tool of the chapter
slides.main: An estimate recalculated taking into account that another has already happened.

captions: The main tool of the chapter is conditional probability
The probability of an event recalculated taking into account that another has already happened
It is cloudy — the probability of rain is higher than on a clear day, although the climate is the same
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B): we squeeze the world down to the cases where B happened and look at the share of A
Almost everything you say about the future is a conditional probability; it is just that the condition is usually not spelled out

frames.text: we recalculate the shares inside the new world
illustrative numbers: the climate is the same

body.text: We squeeze the world down to the cases where B happened and look at the share of A among them: when cloudy, rain is more likely, although the climate is the same.

slides.title: Bayes' theorem
slides.sub: The rule for turning a condition around
slides.main: From an observed effect to the probability of a cause: confidence is updated by data.

captions: Bayes' formula is the rule for turning a condition around
P(cause | effect) = P(effect | cause) · P(cause) / P(effect)
The human reading: we update our confidence when new data appears
The service had crashed before (prior) → monitoring fired (evidence) → now we believe differently (posterior)
Bayes is not a spell but honest bookkeeping of beliefs

body.text: There was a prior confidence — how many times the service had crashed before; evidence arrived — the monitoring fired; it became a posterior. Bayes is honest bookkeeping of beliefs.

slides.title: The trap of the disease
slides.sub: The test is good, the result is deceptive
slides.main: The test catches 99 of 100 sick people, but a positive result is right only 9% of the time.

captions: The famous trap with numbers
The disease is rare: one person in a thousand has it
The test is good: it catches a sick person in 99 of 100 cases, but wrongly flags a healthy one in 1 of 100
The test is positive — what is the probability of the disease?
Intuition screams "99 %", mathematics says ≈ 9 %: per 100 000 — 99 sick caught and about 1 000 false alarms
A positive result more often means an error: there are too many healthy people — this is the power of the base rate, not a defect of the test

frames.text: the base rate outweighs the accuracy of the test

body.text: This is not a defect of the test but the power of the base rate: there are too many healthy people, so a positive result more often means an error than a disease.

slides.title: A Bayesian spam filter
slides.sub: The mechanism all email lives on
slides.main: The filter does not "know" that it is looking at spam — it updates its confidence word by word.

captions: The same mechanism drives the spam filters that all email lives with
The prior probability of spam is the experience of past mail, say every third letter
The word "free" is evidence: among spam it occurs incomparably more often than among normal letters
Bayes multiplies the prior confidence by the word's characteristicness and gives an updated estimate
The filter does not "know" that it is looking at spam — it updates its confidence word by word

frames.text: word by word — the confidence grows

body.text: Bayes multiplies the prior confidence by how characteristic the word is of spam and gives an updated estimate.

slides.title: Base rate neglect
slides.sub: The trap from the paragraph about the disease
slides.main: People estimate how characteristic evidence is quite well, and fail on how common the cause is.

captions: The trap has a name: base rate neglect
People are quite good at estimating how characteristic evidence is of a cause, but fail on the question of how common the cause is overall
Hence practical rules
An alert that fires rarely on a rare event is almost always false — set thresholds taking the prior frequency into account
Rare things are searched for in a cascade: a cheap rough filter first, then an expensive accurate analysis

frames.text: thresholds — taking the prior frequency into account

body.text: Even a perfectly accurate tool for a rare phenomenon produces mostly false alarms.

slides.title: Probability in engineering
slides.main: Decisions about capacity, thresholds and filters are made on numbers, not on gut feeling.

captions: Probabilistic thinking shows up in engineering at every step
Evaluating a cache: probability of a hit × gain − probability of a miss × cost
A Bloom filter: "maybe present" with a controlled error and "definitely absent" without errors — saves millions of database queries
An A/B test is Bayes in the other direction: data accumulates, confidence grows, and we decide when it has passed the threshold
The number of retries and replicas is an estimate of failure probabilities: p² for two independent replicas

frames.text: capacity and eviction — on these numbers
most "no" answers are cut off without a database request
confidence that variant B is better grows with data
at p = 1 % failure of one replica

body.text: The controlled probability of a false "maybe" is the price for which Bloom saves millions of database queries.

slides.title: Bayesian diagnostics
slides.sub: A service went down, five alerts are lit
slides.main: The probability of each cause given the symptoms is the prior frequency times characteristicness.

captions: One more area where Bayes is a workhorse: diagnostics
A service went down, and five alerts lit up on the dashboard
The probability of each cause given these symptoms: the frequency of the failure × how characteristic the symptom is of it
An experienced on-call engineer starts with what breaks more often and better explains the picture; formulas make the intuition reproducible
Good incident documentation is an accumulated table of the prior frequencies of your system

frames.text: the on-call engineer's intuition = a Bayesian estimate
a table of the prior frequencies of your system

body.text: An experienced on-call engineer does this intuitively; formulas make the intuition reproducible, and incident documentation is an accumulated table of the prior frequencies of your system.

slides.title: The summary of the course
slides.main: The course has become your tool: count, prove, traverse and estimate.

captions: Let's sum up — and at the same time close the whole course
Language: sets, relations and combinatorics — describing data and counting options
Logic: predicates and quantifiers formulate statements, induction and recurrences prove them and estimate time
Graphs: vertices, edges and traversals — the frame for DOM trees, dependencies and routes
Probability and Bayes added the most important thing — the ability to reason where there are no guarantees
Now this course is your tool: next comes programming in Python and algorithms, and everything will come to life line by line

body.text: Next — programming in Python and algorithms: there all of it will come to life line by line.
